subject: Endpoint commitment partitioning: TTFT & sustained token-rate exception request
messages:
From: Carmen Lopez <carmen.lopez@cloudline.com>
To: alex_martinez@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 19 Jul 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Clarify commitments for streaming vs sync endpoints

Hi Alex / Marissa,

Quick question as we scope the integration: do your standard SLOs for time-to-first-token and sustained token/sec apply identically to streaming and synchronous (non-streaming) endpoints? Our use case will multiplex long-lived websocket streams and we need to understand whether you can commit to the same TTFT and sustained per-request token throughput for both shapes.

Specifically:
- We expect many requests to ask for 800–2,000 tokens (generation length) over a stream.
- Some clients will rely on a first token arriving under 200ms to render a progressive UI.
- Others care more about sustained token/sec during long generations.

Can you share whether Redwood is willing to (a) keep identical numeric commitments, (b) provide a documented carve-out that documents different commitments for streaming vs sync, or (c) refuse to separate commitments and require the same SLA for all endpoints?

I've attached a short excerpt of our roadmap showing expected peak concurrency. Happy to hop on a call if it's easier.

Thanks,
Carmen
VP Product, Cloudline Labs

Attachment: Cloudline-Roadmap.pdf (summary)

From: alex_martinez@redwood.ai
To: Carmen Lopez <carmen.lopez@cloudline.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 19 Jul 2027 11:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Clarify commitments for streaming vs sync endpoints

Carmen — thanks for the clear note and the roadmap snapshot. TL;DR: we can support a carve-out, but we need to be explicit in contract language and operational controls. Details below.

Background and how we think about it:
- Redwood treats "time-to-first-token" (TTFT) as a delivery metric that depends on request shape and execution path. Synchronous (batch) endpoints typically run on the fast-path optimized for low RTT and short context windows; streaming endpoints often enable additional buffering and chunked generation semantics which can increase the observed TTFT.
- For sustained token/sec we optimize with continuous batching and KV caching; however, long-lived streaming sessions interacting with large context lengths show different throughput profiles, especially when KV cache churn is high.

Our proposal (draft, negotiable):
1) Streaming endpoint carve-out for TTFT: commit to first-token median <= 250ms for streaming endpoints in the production plan, vs median <= 120ms for equivalent synchronous endpoints under the same instance class.
2) Sustained token-rate: for generation durations > 512 tokens we propose a guaranteed sustained delivery floor of 40 tokens/sec (p99 under sustained load conditions defined in appendix), with a target operational baseline of 80 tokens/sec on dedicated capacity.
3) Fallback and observable behaviour: when streaming falls behind we commit to (a) automatic fallback to a compatible model variant (if available) and (b) a streaming-level outage window metric (how long the stream experiences backpressure > 5s).

Operational asks from Cloudline for the carve-out to be feasible:
- Provide a sample traffic trace (per-request token length distribution + concurrency histogram) and expected RPS by hour.
- Agree to per-route rate limits and a token-budget for bursty clients.
- Allow Redwood to enable prefix caching for repeated prompts and provide a path to enable dedicated capacity for strict throughput needs.

Next step: if Cloudline is aligned we'll (1) fill the SLA-exception-form with exact numeric thresholds and traffic profile, (2) route to legal for a short carve-out clause, and (3) schedule a 30-min deep-dive (ops + infra) to confirm observability hooks.

If this sounds reasonable I can draft contract language and push a DocuSign link.

— Alex Martinez
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
 alex_martinez@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0132

Attachment: SLA-exception-form.pdf

From: marissa_cole@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: Clarify commitments for streaming vs sync endpoints

Adding a bit of product/ops color. Alex's recommendation is operationally sound — we do the carve-out frequently for customers with heavy streaming patterns. To make the exception defensible in a contract we need the following filled in on the form:
- Per-route peak concurrency (p95) and expected steady-state concurrency.
- Distribution of requested generation lengths (0–128, 129–512, 513–2048, >2048).
- Whether you need guaranteed throughput on shared hosted plans or are willing to move to Dedicated capacity.
- Allowed fallback behavior (auto-switching model variants, graceful degradation).

I'll attach the exception template and a short example clause for the MSA. Once we have the completed form (and a short sample trace) I'll own the legal/ops thread and drive the carve-out into the statement of work.

Marissa Cole
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.ai

Forwarding the thread with a draft clause (below) for legal review and to share with Cloudline. Carmen — see the attached docx for a redline-friendly clause.

--- Forwarded message ---
From: alex_martinez@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 20 Jul 2027 13:35:00 -0700
Subject: Draft carve-out for streaming endpoints (for review)
To: marissa_cole@redwood.ai

Proposed contract language (draft):
"For streaming endpoints, Redwood Inference will measure 'Time-to-First-Token' (TTFT) and 'Sustained Token Rate' (STR) separately from synchronous endpoint obligations. The Parties agree that the median TTFT for streaming endpoints will not exceed 250ms under the traffic profile and conditions set out in Schedule X. For generation requests with expected output length greater than 512 tokens, Redwood will guarantee a sustained token delivery floor of 40 tokens per second at p99, subject to the operational constraints and fallback policies in Schedule Y. Instances of non-compliance will be handled per the SLA remedies in Section Z, with the exception that credits for streaming-level variance will be capped at 25% of the standard monthly service credit for equivalent synchronous endpoint breaches."

Please advise if legal is comfortable with the fallback wording and the cap on credits. If approved I will share with Carmen and produce a DocuSign-ready exhibit.

— Alex

From: Carmen Lopez <carmen.lopez@cloudline.com>
To: alex_martinez@redwood.ai
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 20 Jul 2027 18:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Draft carve-out for streaming endpoints (for review)

Alex / Marissa — thanks for the clear proposal and the draft clause. Cloudline is comfortable proceeding on that basis with two small edits:
1) Change median TTFT target to 'median <= 220ms' for streaming endpoints (we can accept the sustainability floor of 40 tokens/sec).
2) Remove the explicit 25% cap on streaming credits; we prefer credits tied to observed customer impact language.

If you can route an updated exhibit to DocuSign we'll get this over the legal finish line quickly. Our procurement team is ready to countersign once the exhibit matches the numbers we discussed.

Agreed next steps:
- Alex to share updated exhibit + HubSpot deal update (CL-3892).
- Cloudline to provide a 24-hr sample trace for the July peak.
- Schedule 30-min ops sync Wed/Thu.

Thanks,
Carmen
VP Product, Cloudline Labs
